hints: Count the five carbon atoms in Z and sort them by bonding: which carbon has a triple bond, which has a double bond to oxygen, and which have only single bonds?
walkthrough:
Picture what hybridisation tells you**
Think of hybridisation as a shorthand for how many directions a carbon is bonding in. A carbon with four single bonds points in four directions, that is $sp^3$. A carbon with one double bond points in three directions, that is $sp^2$. A carbon with a triple bond points in two opposite directions, that is $sp$.

Sort the five carbons in Z**
Write Z as $\text{H}_2\text{NCOCH}_2\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$. The nitrile carbon in $-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ has a triple bond, so that is the one $sp$ carbon. The amide carbonyl carbon in $\text{H}_2\text{N-C=O}$ has a double bond to O, so that is the one $sp^2$ carbon. The remaining three carbons, $\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CH}$ and $\text{CH}_2$, all have four single bonds, so they are all $sp^3$.

hints: Look at the three nitrogen containing groups in Z and recall what excess aqueous $\text{HCl}$ with heat does to an amide, a nitrile and a free amine.
walkthrough:
See all three functional groups reacting at once**
Z contains an amide $\text{-CONH}_2$, a primary amine $\text{-NH}_2$ and a nitrile $\text{-CN}$. With excess hot aqueous $\text{HCl}$ more than one change happens in the same mixture.

Separate protonation from breaking bonds**
The $\text{-NH}_2$ simply picks up $\text{H}^+$ to give $\text{-NH}_3^+$, that is acid-base or neutralisation with no carbon skeleton change. The amide $\text{-CONH}_2$ and the nitrile $\text{-CN}$ are both hydrolysed by water in acid to carboxylic acid groups $\text{-COOH}$, that is acid hydrolysis.
Final answer: acid-base / neutralisation and hydrolysis

hints: For each reaction decide which functional groups in Z are attacked and which are left untouched by that reagent.
Recall that hot acid converts both $\text{-CONH}_2$ and $\text{-CN}$ to $\text{-COOH}$ while $\text{-NH}_2$ becomes $\text{-NH}_3^+\text{Cl}^-$.

Recall that $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ selectively acylates the nucleophilic $\text{-NH}_2$ to an amide, and that excess $\text{LiAlH}_4$ reduces $\text{-CONH}_2$ to $\text{-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{-CN}$ to $\text{-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$.
Draw the full carbon chain $\text{C-C-C-C-C}$ for each product and add the new end groups, keeping the central CH unit in place.
walkthrough:
Build reaction 7, complete acid hydrolysis**
Start from $\text{H}_2\text{NCOCH}_2\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$. Hot excess $\text{HCl(aq)}$ hydrolyses the left amide: $\text{H}_2\text{N-C=O + H}_2\text{O + H}^+ \rightarrow \text{HO-C=O + NH}_4^+$. It also hydrolyses the right nitrile: $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N + 2H}_2\text{O + H}^+ \rightarrow \text{-COOH + NH}_4^+$. The middle amine is protonated: $\text{-NH}_2 + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{-NH}_3^+$. The organic product is therefore $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{CH}(\text{NH}_3^+\text{Cl}^-)\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, a dicarboxylic acid with a protonated amine.

Build reaction 8, selective acylation**
$\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ is an acylating agent. The most nucleophilic site in Z is the free primary amine, not the amide nitrogen and not the nitrile. So $\text{-NH}_2 + \text{CH}_3\text{COCl} \rightarrow \text{-NHCOCH}_3 + \text{HCl}$. The amide and nitrile are unchanged. The product is $\text{H}_2\text{NOCCH}_2\text{CH}(\text{NHCOCH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$, containing an amide at the left, a new secondary amide in the middle, and the nitrile still on the right.

Build reaction 9, complete reduction with $\text{LiAlH}_4$**
Excess $\text{LiAlH}_4$ is a powerful reducing agent. It reduces amides to amines: $\text{-CONH}_2 \rightarrow \text{-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. It reduces nitriles to primary amines: $\text{-CN} \rightarrow \text{-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. The existing $\text{-NH}_2$ is unchanged. So the $\text{C=O}$ carbon becomes $\text{CH}_2$ attached to $\text{NH}_2$, and the $\text{CN}$ carbon becomes $\text{CH}_2$ attached to $\text{NH}_2$. The product is the triamine $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$.

hints: Check whether any of the five carbons in $\text{H}_2\text{NCOCH}_2\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$ are in identical environments or related by symmetry.
walkthrough:
Test each carbon for uniqueness**
Carbon-13 NMR gives one peak per unique carbon environment. In Z the five carbons are: amide $\text{C=O}$, $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{C=O}$, $\text{CH}$ next to $\text{NH}_2$, $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{CN}$, and nitrile $\text{CN}$ carbon. There is no symmetry to make any two the same, each neighbour set is different, so all five are inequivalent and give 5 peaks.

hints: Remember that in $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ all $\text{N-H}$ protons exchange away, so only the C-H protons a, b and c are seen, and apply the n+1 rule to neighbours on adjacent carbons.
Use Table 6.3 to match environment a ($\text{CH}_2$ next to C=O), c ($\text{CH}_2$ next to nitrile) and b (CH next to N, coupled to four neighbouring H) to shift ranges.
walkthrough:
Remove the exchangeable protons from the picture**
In $\text{D}_2\text{O}$, $\text{-NH}_2$ and $\text{-CONH}_2$ protons exchange with deuterium and disappear from the $^1\text{H}$ NMR spectrum. You only see the carbon bound protons: a is $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{C=O}$, b is $\text{CH}$ next to $\text{NH}_2$, c is $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{CN}$.

Work out splitting with the n+1 rule**
Proton a ($\text{CH}_2$) has only one neighbour proton set, the single H on b, so n = 1, giving a doublet. Proton c ($\text{CH}_2$) is the same, it sees only the one H on b, so it is also a doublet. Proton b ($\text{CH}$) sees four H in total, two on a plus two on c, so n = 4, giving a quintet which is recorded as a multiplet.

Assign chemical shifts from Table 6.3**
Environment a is alkyl next to $\text{C=O}$, $\text{-CH}_2\text{-C=O}$, range $\delta$ 2.2-3.0. Environment c is alkyl next to nitrile, $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CN}$, range $\delta$ 2.0-3.0. Environment b is on a carbon attached to the electronegative N atom, $\text{-CH}_2\text{-N}$ type, range $\delta$ 3.2-4.0, more deshielded than a and c.
Final answer: a: doublet, $\delta$ 2.2-3.0; b: multiplet, $\delta$ 3.2-4.0; c: doublet, $\delta$ 2.0-3.0
